etymology: From Anglo-Saxon werig, tired, exhausted. Webster 1828: tired; fatigued; made impatient of continuance. Scripture says twice that God can be wearied, and both times names what does it — and once says the incarnate Son was wearied by a walk.
biblical_def: Isaiah puts an accusation in God’s mouth that reverses the expected direction of complaint. Israel had not wearied God with the cost of sacrifices; the reverse: thou hast made me to serve with thy sins, thou hast wearied me with thine iniquities (Isaiah 43:24). Malachi is more specific about the means, and it is words: Ye have wearied the LORD with your words. Yet ye say, Wherein have we wearied him? When ye say, Every one that doeth evil is good in the sight of the LORD, and he delighteth in them; or, Where is the God of judgment? (Malachi 2:17). What wearies God is a people calling evil good and then asking where justice has gone. Isaiah asks the House of David the same question about proportion: Is it a small thing for you to weary men, but will ye weary my God also? (Isaiah 7:13). And then, most startling of all, the word is used of Christ: Jesus therefore, being wearied with his journey, sat thus on the well: and it was about the sixth hour (John 4:6) — the One who does not faint (Isaiah 40:28) sat down tired at noon, and then conducted the longest recorded conversation of His ministry.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines WEARY as to reduce or exhaust the strength by labor or exertion; to tire; to fatigue; to make impatient of continuance; hence WEARIED, tired, fatigued, harassed.
webster_full: WEARY, a. — Having the strength much exhausted by toil or violent exertion; tired; fatigued.
Having the patience exhausted, or the mind yielding to discouragement.
WEARY, v.t. — To reduce or exhaust the strength by labor or exertion; to tire; to fatigue.
To make impatient of continuance; to harass; to tire the patience of.
Anglo-Saxon werig, weary; the verb wergian, to tire.
scriptures: Isaiah 43:24
Thou hast bought me no sweet cane with money, neither hast thou filled me with the fat of thy sacrifices: but thou hast made me to serve with thy sins, thou hast wearied me with thine iniquities.
Malachi 2:17

Ye have wearied the LORD with your words. Yet ye say, Wherein have we wearied him? When ye say, Every one that doeth evil is good in the sight of the LORD, and he delighteth in them; or, Where is the God of judgment?
Isaiah 7:13
And he said, Hear ye now, O house of David; Is it a small thing for you to weary men, but will ye weary my God also?
John 4:6
Now Jacob's well was there. Jesus therefore, being wearied with his journey, sat thus on the well: and it was about the sixth hour.
corruption_summary: Malachi 2:17 identifies what wearies God as the declaration that those who do evil are good in His sight, which is precisely the affirmation modern religion has learned to offer as compassion.
corruption_paragraphs: Every one that doeth evil is good in the sight of the LORD, and he delighteth in them; or, Where is the God of judgment? Malachi records two sentences and they belong together: God approves of what He has forbidden, and there is no judgment coming. This is not ancient cynicism only; it is the settled position of a great deal of contemporary Western religion, arrived at not by argument but by attrition, and generally presented as compassion rather than as doctrine. The prophet’s reply comes in the next verse and it is the messenger of the covenant, who shall sit as a refiner and purifier of silver. To say that God delights in what He has called sin is to weary Him, and the answer to it is not softer language but the coming of the One who purifies.

John 4:6 belongs to the doctrine of the incarnation and should not be softened either. The Son who upholds all things by the word of His power sat down at a well because He was tired from walking, and Isaiah 40:28 says of God that He fainteth not, neither is weary. Both are true, and the Chalcedonian definition is what holds them: one Person in two natures, without confusion, change, division or separation. He was wearied in His humanity and not in His deity, and the humanity was not a costume. This matters practically. Hebrews 4:15 grounds our access on a High Priest touched with the feeling of our infirmities, and the tired man on the well kerb at noon is the evidence. He did not conserve Himself; He spent the rest of the sixth hour on a Samaritan woman with five husbands.
roots_summary: Hebrew yaga (H3021), to toil, to grow weary; laah (H3811), to be exhausted or impatient; Greek kopiao (G2872), to labour to the point of exhaustion.
roots_lines: Hebrew yaga (H3021) — to toil until weary; thou hast wearied me with thine iniquities (Isaiah 43:24) and Malachi 2:17.
Hebrew laah (H3811) — to be weary, to be impatient of; will ye weary my God also? (Isaiah 7:13).
Greek kopiao (G2872) — to grow weary from labour; being wearied with his journey (John 4:6).
Hebrew malak (H4397) with berith — the messenger of the covenant, Malachi’s answer to the wearying (Malachi 3:1).
Greek sumpatheo (G4834) — to be touched with the feeling of; the High Priest of Hebrews 4:15.
usage: Thou hast wearied me with thine iniquities (Isaiah 43:24) — the complaint runs the opposite way from the expected one.
Ye have wearied the LORD with your words (Malachi 2:17) — and the words are that evil is good and judgment is absent.
Jesus therefore, being wearied with his journey, sat thus on the well (John 4:6) — and then spent the hour on one Samaritan woman.

etymology: From Anglo-Saxon hindrian, to keep back, from hinder, behind. Webster 1828: to stop or to prevent from proceeding; to obstruct; to impede. Paul surrenders a right rather than hinder the gospel, and Peter says a husband can hinder his own prayers.
biblical_def: Paul had an apostolic right to material support and refused to use it, giving one reason: we have not used this power; but suffer all things, lest we should hinder the gospel of Christ (1 Corinthians 9:12). The right was real, and he laid it down because exercising it might have obstructed the message. Peter applies the same verb to the domestic life of a Christian husband, with a consequence that should stop any man reading it: ye husbands, dwell with them according to knowledge, giving honour unto the wife, as unto the weaker vessel, and as being heirs together of the grace of life; that your prayers be not hindered (1 Peter 3:7). How a man treats his wife determines whether his prayers get through. Our Lord charges the lawyers with hindering others from an entrance they themselves declined: ye have taken away the key of knowledge: ye entered not in yourselves, and them that were entering in ye hindered (Luke 11:52). And Paul asks the Galatians the question a runner’s coach asks: Ye did run well; who did hinder you that ye should not obey the truth? (Galatians 5:7).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines HINDER as to stop, or to prevent from proceeding; to obstruct; to impede; to embarrass; to retard or check.
webster_full: HINDER, v.t. — To stop, or to prevent from proceeding; to obstruct; to interrupt.
To impede; to retard; to check in progressing.
To prevent; to keep back; with from.
HINDER, a. — That is behind; posterior; as the hinder part of a ship.
Anglo-Saxon hindrian, from hinder, behind.
scriptures: 1 Corinthians 9:12
If others be partakers of this power over you, are not we rather? Nevertheless we have not used this power; but suffer all things, lest we should hinder the gospel of Christ.
1 Peter 3:7

Likewise, ye husbands, dwell with them according to knowledge, giving honour unto the wife, as unto the weaker vessel, and as being heirs together of the grace of life; that your prayers be not hindered.
Luke 11:52
Woe unto you, lawyers! for ye have taken away the key of knowledge: ye entered not in yourselves, and them that were entering in ye hindered.
Galatians 5:7
Ye did run well; who did hinder you that ye should not obey the truth?
corruption_summary: 1 Peter 3:7 attaches a man’s prayers to his treatment of his wife, which is a far harder complementarianism than either its critics or some of its advocates describe.
corruption_paragraphs: The verse is often read only for the phrase the weaker vessel and then argued about. Its actual weight falls elsewhere. Peter commands husbands to dwell with their wives according to knowledge — to study them, not merely to lead them — to give them honour, and to regard them as heirs together of the grace of life, which is a statement of full spiritual equality in the same sentence as the ordering. And he attaches a sanction that has no parallel: a man who fails here will find his prayers hindered. The headship this dictionary holds (Ephesians 5:22-33; 1 Timothy 2:11-15) is defined by texts like this one, and it is the opposite of the caricature its critics attack and of the entitlement some of its advocates practise. The man bears the heavier accountability, and God will not hear him while his wife is dishonoured.

1 Corinthians 9 is the neglected half of the argument about Christian liberty. Paul spends the chapter establishing his rights — to support, to lead about a wife, to forbear working — and then says he has used none of them, lest the gospel be hindered. The reasoning is not that the rights were doubtful but that a right may be surrendered when its exercise would obstruct the message. This cuts against the reflex, common in a rights-conscious age and now common in the church, of treating every legitimate liberty as a thing to be defended wherever it is questioned. Romans 14 makes the same point about the weaker brother. Liberty is real, and it is precisely because it is real that it can be laid down.
roots_summary: Greek egkope (G1464), a cutting in, an obstruction; egkopto (G1465), to cut into, to impede; koluo (G2967), to forbid or prevent; anakopto, to beat back.
roots_lines: Greek egkope (G1464) — a cutting in, an obstruction placed in a road; lest we should hinder the gospel (1 Corinthians 9:12).
Greek egkopto (G1465) — to cut into or impede; that your prayers be not hindered (1 Peter 3:7) and who did hinder you (Galatians 5:7).
Greek koluo (G2967) — to forbid, to hinder; them that were entering in ye hindered (Luke 11:52).
Greek sunkleronomos (G4789) — joint-heir; heirs together of the grace of life (1 Peter 3:7).
Greek exousia (G1849) — authority, right, power; the right Paul declined to use (1 Corinthians 9:12).
usage: Lest we should hinder the gospel of Christ (1 Corinthians 9:12) — a real right laid down because its use might obstruct.
That your prayers be not hindered (1 Peter 3:7) — a man’s prayers tied to his treatment of his wife.
Ye entered not in yourselves, and them that were entering in ye hindered (Luke 11:52) — the key taken away by those who would not use it.

etymology: From hap, chance or fortune, of Norse origin. Webster 1828: came by chance; fell out; occurred. The English word carries an assumption of randomness that Scripture consistently denies, and Paul uses it of the events that furthered the gospel.
biblical_def: The Philistine lords devise a test precisely to distinguish chance from judgment: see, if it goeth up by the way of his own coast to Bethshemesh, then he hath done us this great evil: but if not, then we shall know that it is not his hand that smote us: it was a chance that happened to us (1 Samuel 6:9). They set two milch kine, unbroken and separated from their calves, before a cart; the cows went straight to Bethshemesh, lowing as they went. The test was fair and it settled the question. Paul uses the word of his own imprisonment and immediately overrules the sense of accident: the things which happened unto me have fallen out rather unto the furtherance of the gospel (Philippians 1:12) — the chains produced a hearing in the palace and boldness in the brethren. He uses it again of Israel’s condition, and calls it a mystery with a stated term: blindness in part is happened to Israel, until the fulness of the Gentiles be come in (Romans 11:25). Luke uses it plainly of the road to Emmaus: they talked together of all these things which had happened (Luke 24:14).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines HAPPEN as to come by chance; to come without one’s previous expectation; to fall out; to come; to occur; hence HAPPENED, come to pass, occurred, fallen out.
webster_full: HAPPEN, v.i. — To come by chance; to come without one’s previous expectation; to fall out.
To come; to befall; as, misfortunes happen to all men.
To light; to fall or come unexpectedly; as, he happened to be present.
HAP, n. — That which comes suddenly or unexpectedly; chance; fortune; accident.
From hap, Old Norse happ, chance — the root of happy, haply, perhaps, mishap.
scriptures: 1 Samuel 6:9

And see, if it goeth up by the way of his own coast to Bethshemesh, then he hath done us this great evil: but if not, then we shall know that it is not his hand that smote us: it was a chance that happened to us.
Philippians 1:12
But I would ye should understand, brethren, that the things which happened unto me have fallen out rather unto the furtherance of the gospel;
Romans 11:25

For I would not, brethren, that ye should be ignorant of this mystery, lest ye should be wise in your own conceits; that blindness in part is happened to Israel, until the fulness of the Gentiles be come in.
Luke 24:14
And they talked together of all these things which had happened.
corruption_summary: The English word assumes chance, and Scripture denies that anything falls out by chance — a denial the biblical writers make while still using the ordinary vocabulary of everyday speech.
corruption_paragraphs: Happen descends from hap, meaning chance, and the assumption is built into the word. Scripture uses such ordinary language and then denies what it implies. Proverbs 16:33 says the lot is cast into the lap but the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD; our Lord says a sparrow does not fall to the ground without the Father, and the very hairs of the head are numbered (Matthew 10:29-30). The Philistines in 1 Samuel 6 were right to think the question worth testing, and God answered their test. The Reformed doctrine of providence holds that God upholds, directs, disposes and governs all creatures and things, from the greatest to the least, and that nothing occurs by chance or outside His governance — while genuinely employing means and second causes, so that the ordinary language of things happening remains truthful at its own level.

Philippians 1:12 is the pastoral use of the doctrine and it is worth stating carefully. Paul does not say his imprisonment was pleasant, nor that he understood it at the time, nor that all imprisonments serve the gospel. He reports an outcome he could see: the palace guard had heard, and the brethren were emboldened. This is the honest form of the doctrine of providence — the believer confesses that God governs everything, and he reports what he can actually observe of it, without inventing reasons for what he cannot see. Romans 8:28 promises that all things work together for good to them that love God; it does not promise that the working will be visible on demand, and the difference between those two claims is the difference between faith and speculation.
roots_summary: Hebrew miqreh (H4745), a chance or accident; qarah (H7136), to meet or befall; Greek sumbaino (G4819), to come together, to happen; ginomai (G1096), to become or come to pass.
roots_lines: Hebrew miqreh (H4745) — a chance or accident; it was a chance that happened to us (1 Samuel 6:9).
Hebrew qarah (H7136) — to meet, to befall; the verb behind the noun, and behind Ruth’s hap in Ruth 2:3.
Greek sumbaino (G4819) — to come together, to happen; the things which happened unto me (Philippians 1:12).
Greek ginomai (G1096) — to become, to come to pass; the ordinary New Testament verb for events occurring.
Greek porosis (G4457) — a hardening or callus; the blindness in part of Romans 11:25.
usage: It was a chance that happened to us (1 Samuel 6:9) — the hypothesis the Philistines set out to test, and God answered it.
The things which happened unto me have fallen out rather unto the furtherance of the gospel (Philippians 1:12) — an outcome reported, not a reason invented.
Blindness in part is happened to Israel, until the fulness of the Gentiles be come in (Romans 11:25) — a condition with a stated term.

etymology: From Latin consultare, to deliberate, frequentative of consulere, to take counsel. Webster 1828: asked advice of; deliberated together. The Gospels use it twice of the chief priests deliberating a murder, and Chronicles once of a king deliberating a choir.
biblical_def: The same verb serves two councils with opposite objects. Matthew records the Sanhedrin’s deliberation: consulted that they might take Jesus by subtilty, and kill him (Matthew 26:4). John records a second and stranger one, provoked by an inconvenient miracle: the chief priests consulted that they might put Lazarus also to death (John 12:10) — a man raised from the dead was evidence, and the solution proposed was to kill him again. Deliberation is not virtue; it is only a method, and it will serve any end. Against that, Chronicles records Jehoshaphat facing an invading army: when he had consulted with the people, he appointed singers unto the LORD, and that should praise the beauty of holiness, as they went out before the army, and to say, Praise the LORD; for his mercy endureth for ever (2 Chronicles 20:21). A war council that produces a choir. And Nehemiah, confronting usury among the returned exiles, deliberates alone before acting: Then I consulted with myself, and I rebuked the nobles, and the rulers (Nehemiah 5:7).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines CONSULT as to seek the opinion or advice of another; to ask advice of; to deliberate together; to take counsel in order to form a plan.
webster_full: CONSULT, v.i. — To seek the opinion or advice of another, by a statement of facts and suitable inquiries.
To take counsel together; to seek opinions and information by mutual discussion.
CONSULT, v.t. — To ask advice of; to seek the opinion of, as a guide to conduct.
To plan, devise or contrive; as, to consult the ruin of a state.
Latin consultare, frequentative of consulo, to take counsel — the root of counsel and consul.
scriptures: Matthew 26:4
And consulted that they might take Jesus by subtilty, and kill him.
John 12:10
But the chief priests consulted that they might put Lazarus also to death;
2 Chronicles 20:21

And when he had consulted with the people, he appointed singers unto the LORD, and that should praise the beauty of holiness, as they went out before the army, and to say, Praise the LORD; for his mercy endureth for ever.
Nehemiah 5:7
Then I consulted with myself, and I rebuked the nobles, and the rulers, and said unto them, Ye exact usury, every one of his brother.
corruption_summary: John 12:10 shows a council responding to unanswerable evidence by proposing to destroy it, which is the standing behaviour of unbelief and not a failure of information.
corruption_paragraphs: Lazarus was alive, publicly known, and had been four days dead. The chief priests did not dispute the fact; the previous chapter records them acknowledging that this man does many miracles (John 11:47). Their deliberation was about the consequence — that many of the Jews went away and believed — and their proposal was to kill the evidence. This is the clearest case in Scripture that unbelief is moral rather than evidential. Our Lord had said as much in the parable: neither will they be persuaded, though one rose from the dead (Luke 16:31), and here the parable is enacted by the men who heard it. The apologetic consequence is worth stating plainly. Evidence has its proper use and Scripture appeals to it constantly; but no accumulation of it converts a will that has decided, and the new birth is not the conclusion of an argument.

2 Chronicles 20 is the best answer in Scripture to the charge that faith is passivity. Jehoshaphat proclaimed a fast, gathered the nation, prayed a prayer that rehearses the covenant and ends neither know we what to do: but our eyes are upon thee (2 Chronicles 20:12), received a word through Jahaziel, consulted with the people, and then appointed singers to go out before the army. He did not stay home; the army marched. What he did was order the campaign around the conviction that the battle was God’s, and the singers went first. The Reformed doctrine of providence has always insisted on the use of means, and this chapter shows means employed by a man who had genuinely stopped relying on them.
roots_summary: Greek sumbouleuo (G4823), to take counsel together; bouleuo (G1011), to deliberate or resolve; Hebrew yaats (H3289), to advise or counsel; malak (H4427), to take counsel with oneself.
roots_lines: Greek sumbouleuo (G4823) — to take counsel together; the Sanhedrin’s deliberation (Matthew 26:4).
Greek bouleuo (G1011) — to deliberate, to resolve upon; the plan against Lazarus (John 12:10).
Hebrew yaats (H3289) — to advise, to counsel; when he had consulted with the people (2 Chronicles 20:21).
Hebrew malak (H4427) — to consult or take counsel with oneself; Then I consulted with myself (Nehemiah 5:7).
Hebrew hadrath qodesh — the beauty of holiness; what Jehoshaphat’s singers were appointed to praise.
usage: Consulted that they might take Jesus by subtilty, and kill him (Matthew 26:4) — deliberation is a method, and it will serve any end.
The chief priests consulted that they might put Lazarus also to death (John 12:10) — the proposal was to kill the evidence.
When he had consulted with the people, he appointed singers unto the LORD (2 Chronicles 20:21) — a war council that produced a choir.

etymology: From Latin expirare, to breathe out, from ex and spirare, to breathe. Webster 1828: breathed out; came to an end; ceased. In Scripture it marks the completion of appointed terms, and the terms are always God’s.
biblical_def: The word marks a period reaching its appointed end, and Scripture uses it for spans God has fixed. Stephen dates the burning bush by it: when forty years were expired, there appeared to him in the wilderness of mount Sina an angel of the Lord in a flame of fire in a bush (Acts 7:30) — forty years in Pharaoh’s house, forty in Midian, forty in the wilderness, and none of the three shortened. Nathan uses it of David’s life in the promise of the everlasting throne: when thy days be expired that thou must go to be with thy fathers, that I will raise up thy seed after thee (1 Chronicles 17:11). Esther dates a feast by it: when these days were expired, the king made a feast unto all the people that were present in Shushan the palace (Esther 1:5). And Revelation uses it of the term set on the adversary’s confinement: when the thousand years are expired, Satan shall be loosed out of his prison (Revelation 20:7). Even the loosing is on a schedule, and the schedule is not his.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines EXPIRE as to breathe out; to emit the breath; to die; and of time, to come to an end, to close, to conclude, as a period.
webster_full: EXPIRE, v.t. — To breathe out; to throw out the breath from the lungs.
EXPIRE, v.i. — To emit the last breath; to die.
To perish; to end; to fail or be destroyed.
To come to an end; to close or conclude, as a given period; as, a lease has expired.
Latin expirare, from ex, out, and spiro, to breathe — the root of spirit and inspire.
scriptures: Acts 7:30
And when forty years were expired, there appeared to him in the wilderness of mount Sina an angel of the Lord in a flame of fire in a bush.
1 Chronicles 17:11
And it shall come to pass, when thy days be expired that thou must go to be with thy fathers, that I will raise up thy seed after thee, which shall be of thy sons; and I will establish his kingdom.
Revelation 20:7
And when the thousand years are expired, Satan shall be loosed out of his prison,
Esther 1:5

And when these days were expired, the king made a feast unto all the people that were present in Shushan the palace, both unto great and small, seven days, in the court of the garden of the king's palace;
corruption_summary: Revelation 20:7 has Satan loosed only when a term God appointed expires, which is fatal to any dualism that treats the adversary as an independent power.
corruption_paragraphs: Whatever a reader concludes about the millennium, Revelation 20 is unambiguous on one point: the adversary is bound, sealed, and then loosed at the expiry of a term he did not set. Scripture nowhere presents a contest between two comparable powers. Satan is a creature, was cast down, must ask permission concerning Job, must desire to have Peter, and here is imprisoned and released on a schedule. The dualism of Zoroastrian or Manichaean type — two eternal principles at war — has never been Christian, and its popular survival in the imagination of many believers, who picture God and the devil as roughly matched contenders, does real damage to prayer and to peace. On the millennial question itself the dictionary remains open among the historic positions, amillennial, postmillennial and historic premillennial, while rejecting the dispensational system as a nineteenth-century novelty.

Acts 7:30 rewards attention to Stephen’s arithmetic. Moses was forty when he visited his brethren and killed the Egyptian, forty years passed in Midian before the bush, and forty more in the wilderness. Eighty years of preparation for forty years of service, and the second forty were spent keeping another man’s sheep in a desert. Nothing in the record suggests Moses understood the delay at the time; Exodus 2 leaves him simply content to dwell with the man. The doctrine here is not that all delay is preparation — Scripture does not say that — but that God’s terms expire on His calendar and not on ours, and that the man in Midian was not being wasted. Galatians 4:4 states the same principle at the centre of history: when the fulness of the time was come, God sent forth His Son.
roots_summary: Greek pleroo (G4137), to fill up or complete; teleo (G5055), to finish or bring to an end; Hebrew male (H4390), to be full or completed; Aramaic shelam, to be finished.
roots_lines: Greek pleroo (G4137) — to fill up, to complete; when forty years were expired (Acts 7:30).
Greek teleo (G5055) — to bring to an end, to finish; when the thousand years are expired (Revelation 20:7).
Hebrew male (H4390) — to be full, to be completed; when thy days be expired (1 Chronicles 17:11).
Greek pleroma (G4138) — fulness; the fulness of the time (Galatians 4:4).
Hebrew yom (H3117) — a day; the unit of the terms God appoints and closes.
usage: When forty years were expired (Acts 7:30) — eighty years of preparation, and none of it shortened.
When the thousand years are expired, Satan shall be loosed out of his prison (Revelation 20:7) — even the loosing is on a schedule not his own.
When thy days be expired that thou must go to be with thy fathers (1 Chronicles 17:11) — a term closed, and a throne established.

etymology: Past tense of overtake, from over and take: to come up with in pursuit. Webster 1828: came up with in a course, pursuit or journey. In Exodus the Egyptians overtake Israel at the sea, and in Amos the reaper is overtaken by the plowman in a picture of plenty.
biblical_def: The most consequential overtaking in Scripture is a trap that turns into a deliverance: the Egyptians pursued after them, all the horses and chariots of Pharaoh, and his horsemen, and his army, and overtook them encamping by the sea (Exodus 14:9). Israel is caught between an army and deep water, in a position God Himself had directed them into (Exodus 14:2), and the stated purpose was that He would be honoured upon Pharaoh. Laban overtakes Jacob after a seven-day pursuit and is warned in a dream not to speak good or bad to him: Then Laban overtook Jacob. Now Jacob had pitched his tent in the mount (Genesis 31:25). Lamentations uses the word of a nation with nowhere to run: she dwelleth among the heathen, she findeth no rest: all her persecutors overtook her between the straits (Lamentations 1:3). And Amos uses the same verb for an overtaking that is pure blessing: the plowman shall overtake the reaper, and the treader of grapes him that soweth seed (Amos 9:13) — the harvest so great that the next ploughing begins before the reaping is done.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines OVERTAKE as to come up with in a course, pursuit, progress or motion; to catch; and figuratively, to come upon suddenly or unexpectedly, as calamity.
webster_full: OVERTAKE, v.t. — To come up with in a course, pursuit, progress or motion; to catch.
To come upon; to fall on afterwards; as, vengeance overtook him.
To take by surprise; as, to be overtaken in a fault.
OVERTOOK, pret. — Came up with; caught in pursuit.
From over and take; compare the Anglo-Saxon ofertacan.
scriptures: Exodus 14:9
But the Egyptians pursued after them, all the horses and chariots of Pharaoh, and his horsemen, and his army, and overtook them encamping by the sea, beside Pihahiroth, before Baalzephon.
Genesis 31:25
Then Laban overtook Jacob. Now Jacob had pitched his tent in the mount: and Laban with his brethren pitched in the mount of Gilead.
Lamentations 1:3
Judah is gone into captivity because of affliction, and because of great servitude: she dwelleth among the heathen, she findeth no rest: all her persecutors overtook her between the straits.
Amos 9:13

Behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that the plowman shall overtake the reaper, and the treader of grapes him that soweth seed; and the mountains shall drop sweet wine, and all the hills shall melt.
corruption_summary: Exodus 14 has God deliberately positioning His people where they can be overtaken, which no theology that equates divine goodness with the avoidance of hardship can accommodate.
corruption_paragraphs: Exodus 14:2 records the LORD instructing Moses to have Israel turn and encamp before Pihahiroth, between Migdol and the sea — a position with water at their backs and no route of escape — and verse 4 states the reason: I will be honoured upon Pharaoh, and upon all his host. The trap was arranged. Israel’s reaction is the ordinary human one: they cried out, accused Moses of bringing them to die in the wilderness, and said it had been better to serve the Egyptians. The doctrine here is unwelcome and unavoidable. God sometimes leads His people into positions from which only He can deliver them, and does so for the sake of His own glory and their knowledge of Him. Any account of divine goodness that requires God to keep His people out of such positions is contradicted by the central deliverance of the Old Testament.

Amos 9:13 shows the same verb in its happiest use and closes the darkest of the minor prophets. Amos has spent eight chapters on judgment — the plumbline, the basket of summer fruit, the famine of hearing the words of the LORD — and ends with plenty so extravagant that the agricultural calendar collapses: the plowman overtakes the reaper because the harvest has not finished before the next sowing must begin. James cites the preceding verses at the Jerusalem council as fulfilled in the ingathering of the Gentiles (Acts 15:16-17). The pattern is worth marking: the prophets who speak most severely of judgment are the ones who end with the most extravagant restoration, and both are the word of the same God.
roots_summary: Hebrew nasag (H5381), to reach or overtake; radaph (H7291), to pursue; dabaq (H1692), to cling or overtake closely; Greek katalambano (G2638), to seize or overtake.
roots_lines: Hebrew nasag (H5381) — to reach, to overtake; the Egyptians at the sea (Exodus 14:9) and the plowman in Amos 9:13.
Hebrew radaph (H7291) — to pursue; the companion verb of the pursuit that precedes the overtaking.
Hebrew dabaq (H1692) — to cling, to overtake closely; Laban’s seven-day pursuit (Genesis 31:23).
Hebrew metsar (H4712) — a strait or narrow place; overtook her between the straits (Lamentations 1:3).
Greek katalambano (G2638) — to lay hold of, to overtake; the New Testament counterpart term.
usage: Overtook them encamping by the sea (Exodus 14:9) — in a position God Himself had directed them into.
All her persecutors overtook her between the straits (Lamentations 1:3) — a nation with nowhere left to run.
The plowman shall overtake the reaper (Amos 9:13) — the same verb, and the harvest outrunning the calendar.

etymology: From Anglo-Saxon utemest, from ut, out, with a double superlative ending. Webster 1828: extreme; being in the greatest or highest degree; farthest. Jacob’s blessing on Joseph reaches to the utmost bound of the everlasting hills.
biblical_def: Jacob’s blessing on Joseph is the longest and most extravagant in Genesis 49, and it measures itself against geology: The blessings of thy father have prevailed above the blessings of my progenitors unto the utmost bound of the everlasting hills: they shall be on the head of Joseph, and on the crown of the head of him that was separate from his brethren (Genesis 49:26). The blessing outreaches the hills and outlasts the fathers. Jeremiah uses the word for the far edges of the known world in a warning that circumcision of the flesh saves no one: Egypt, and Judah, and Edom, and the children of Ammon, and Moab, and all that are in the utmost corners... for all these nations are uncircumcised, and all the house of Israel are uncircumcised in the heart (Jeremiah 9:26). Israel is listed among the nations, and the distinguishing mark is inward. Balak takes Balaam up to see only a portion of what he means to curse: he brought him up into the high places of Baal, that thence he might see the utmost part of the people (Numbers 22:41) — and the man hired to curse blessed them three times instead.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines UTMOST as extreme; being in the greatest or highest degree; farthest; most distant; and as a noun, the most that can be, the greatest power or degree.
webster_full: UTMOST, a. — Extreme; being in the greatest or highest degree; as the utmost extent.
Farthest; most distant; as the utmost bound.
UTMOST, n. — The most that can be; the greatest power, degree or effort.
UTTERMOST, a. — Of the same sense, and used interchangeably in older English.
Anglo-Saxon utemest, from ut, out, with the doubled superlative -m-est.
scriptures: Genesis 49:26

The blessings of thy father have prevailed above the blessings of my progenitors unto the utmost bound of the everlasting hills: they shall be on the head of Joseph, and on the crown of the head of him that was separate from his brethren.
Jeremiah 9:26

Egypt, and Judah, and Edom, and the children of Ammon, and Moab, and all that are in the utmost corners, that dwell in the wilderness: for all these nations are uncircumcised, and all the house of Israel are uncircumcised in the heart.
Numbers 22:41
And it came to pass on the morrow, that Balak took Balaam, and brought him up into the high places of Baal, that thence he might see the utmost part of the people.
Jeremiah 9:25
Behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that I will punish all them which are circumcised with the uncircumcised;
corruption_summary: Jeremiah 9:26 lists Israel among the uncircumcised nations and locates the real circumcision in the heart, which forecloses every version of salvation by covenant membership.
corruption_paragraphs: Jeremiah names Egypt, Judah, Edom, Ammon, Moab and the wilderness tribes in one breath and says all these nations are uncircumcised — and all the house of Israel are uncircumcised in the heart. The mark in the flesh, given by God and rightly kept, availed nothing where the heart was untouched, and the prophet puts Judah in a list with Moab to make the point unmissable. Paul makes the identical argument in Romans 2:28-29: he is not a Jew which is one outwardly, and circumcision is that of the heart, in the spirit. The application reaches every form of the assumption that covenant standing, church membership, baptism or ancestry secures a man. The Reformed doctrine of the visible and invisible church rests on exactly this distinction, and Jeremiah is where it is stated most bluntly.

Numbers 22-24 is worth reading for what it says about the limits of hostility. Balak takes Balaam to three vantage points, each time hoping a partial view will make cursing easier, and each time the prophet blesses. Balaam was no saint — Scripture is severe about him, naming the way of Balaam and the doctrine of Balaam (2 Peter 2:15; Revelation 2:14), and he ultimately taught Balak to seduce Israel by other means. But he could not curse whom God had not cursed. The doctrine is stated in the passage itself: God is not a man, that he should lie (Numbers 23:19). No hostility, purchased or sincere, can undo what God has spoken over His people; when Israel fell it was by seduction into sin, not by a curse, and that remains the pattern of the adversary’s method.
roots_summary: Hebrew taavah (H8379), a boundary or limit; qatsah (H7098), an extremity or end; qatsats (H7112), cut off, in the phrase for the utmost corners; olam (H5769), everlasting.
roots_lines: Hebrew taavah (H8379) — a limit or boundary; the utmost bound of the everlasting hills (Genesis 49:26).
Hebrew olam (H5769) — long duration, everlasting; the hills against which the blessing is measured.
Hebrew qatsats (H7112) — cut off, clipped at the corners; the idiom rendered utmost corners (Jeremiah 9:26).
Hebrew qatseh (H7097) — an end or extremity; the utmost part of the people (Numbers 22:41).
Hebrew arel (H6189) — uncircumcised; applied by Jeremiah to the heart of Israel.
usage: Unto the utmost bound of the everlasting hills (Genesis 49:26) — a blessing measured against geology and found larger.
All the house of Israel are uncircumcised in the heart (Jeremiah 9:26) — Judah listed among the nations.
That thence he might see the utmost part of the people (Numbers 22:41) — a partial view, sought to make cursing easier.

etymology: The archaic second person singular past of bring, from Anglo-Saxon bringan with the -est ending. Webster 1828 records the form as the second person of the preterit. In Scripture it is nearly always addressed to God about the exodus — and once, damningly, to Moses.
biblical_def: The form belongs to direct address, and in Scripture the One usually addressed is God about His deliverance of Israel. Nehemiah’s great prayer of national confession begins with it: Thou art the LORD the God, who didst choose Abram, and broughtest him forth out of Ur of the Chaldees, and gavest him the name of Abraham (Nehemiah 9:7). The psalmist uses it to name an outcome after an ordeal: Thou hast caused men to ride over our heads; we went through fire and through water: but thou broughtest us out into a wealthy place (Psalm 66:12) — through, not around. Moses uses it in intercession, arguing from God’s reputation among the nations: Lest the land whence thou broughtest us out say, Because the LORD was not able to bring them into the land which he promised them (Deuteronomy 9:28). And at the calf God uses the word against Moses, disowning the people by handing them to him: Go, get thee down; for thy people, which thou broughtest out of the land of Egypt, have corrupted themselves (Exodus 32:7) — thy people, whom thou broughtest out, and Moses spends the rest of the chapter giving them back.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 records BROUGHTEST as the second person singular of the preterit of BRING — to bear, convey, or lead from a distant place to one nearer.
webster_full: BRING, v.t. — To fetch; to bear, convey or lead from a distant to a nearer place.
To produce; to procure as a cause; to draw to.
To cause to come; to induce to a particular state or condition.
BROUGHT, pret. and pp. — of BRING.
BROUGHTEST, the second person singular of the preterit, used in direct address; now archaic.
scriptures: Nehemiah 9:7
Thou art the LORD the God, who didst choose Abram, and broughtest him forth out of Ur of the Chaldees, and gavest him the name of Abraham;
Psalm 66:12
Thou hast caused men to ride over our heads; we went through fire and through water: but thou broughtest us out into a wealthy place.
Deuteronomy 9:28

Lest the land whence thou broughtest us out say, Because the LORD was not able to bring them into the land which he promised them, and because he hated them, he hath brought them out to slay them in the wilderness.
Exodus 32:7
And the LORD said unto Moses, Go, get thee down; for thy people, which thou broughtest out of the land of Egypt, have corrupted themselves:
corruption_summary: The archaic second person singular preserves a distinction modern English has lost — thou to one, ye to many — and its loss flattens a great deal of Scripture, including whom exactly Christ is addressing.
corruption_paragraphs: Broughtest is a second person singular form, and the Authorized Version’s pronouns are precise where modern English cannot be: thou, thee, thy, thine are always singular; ye, you, your are always plural. This is not archaism for its own sake but preserved information. When our Lord tells Peter Satan hath desired to have you (plural, all the disciples) but I have prayed for thee (singular, Peter alone), Luke 22:31-32 carries a distinction that collapses in a modern rendering. The same applies to Exodus 32:7, where God says thy people whom thou broughtest out, singling Moses out. This dictionary is not KJV-only and acknowledges other faithful translations; but the pronoun system is a real advantage of the Authorized Version, and readers who dismiss it as mere quaintness are giving up data.

Exodus 32:7 is one of the most searching moments in the Pentateuch. God calls Israel thy people, which thou broughtest out — language that hands them to Moses and disowns them — and offers to make of Moses a great nation instead. Moses refuses the offer and argues back, on two grounds: the Egyptians will say God brought them out to slay them, and God swore by Himself to Abraham, Isaac and Israel. He pleads God’s reputation and God’s oath, not Israel’s merit, of which there was none that morning. This is the pattern of biblical intercession, and it is the pattern of a greater Mediator: Christ does not plead our worthiness but His own finished work, and the ground of our standing is the covenant God swore with Himself.
roots_summary: Hebrew yatsa (H3318) in the hiphil, to bring out; alah (H5927) in the hiphil, to bring up; the -est ending marks the second person singular in Early Modern English.
roots_lines: Hebrew yatsa (H3318), hiphil — to cause to go out, to bring forth; the standing exodus verb (Exodus 32:7; Deuteronomy 9:28).
Hebrew alah (H5927), hiphil — to bring up; used interchangeably of the deliverance from Egypt.
Hebrew Ur Kasdim — Ur of the Chaldees, whence Abram was brought (Nehemiah 9:7).
Hebrew revayah (H7310) — abundance, a place of overflow; a wealthy place (Psalm 66:12).
English -est — the second person singular ending, matching the singular pronoun thou.
usage: Broughtest him forth out of Ur of the Chaldees (Nehemiah 9:7) — national confession beginning with God’s election of one man.
We went through fire and through water: but thou broughtest us out into a wealthy place (Psalm 66:12) — through, not around.
Thy people, which thou broughtest out of the land of Egypt (Exodus 32:7) — God handing Israel to Moses, and Moses handing them back.

etymology: From Middle English agon, past participle of agon, to go away, from Anglo-Saxon agan. Webster 1828: past; gone; as, a year ago. Our Lord uses it in a judgment on cities that had seen more than Tyre and Sidon ever did.
biblical_def: The word measures elapsed time, and our Lord uses it in one of the most sobering statements in the Gospels: Woe unto thee, Chorazin! woe unto thee, Bethsaida! for if the mighty works, which were done in you, had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago in sackcloth and ashes (Matthew 11:21). Two pagan cities under prophetic condemnation would have repented on evidence that two Galilean towns saw and shrugged at. Paul uses the word with unusual reticence about his own experience: I knew a man in Christ above fourteen years ago, (whether in the body, I cannot tell; or whether out of the body, I cannot tell: God knoweth;) such an one caught up to the third heaven (2 Corinthians 12:2) — fourteen years of silence about the most extraordinary thing that ever happened to him. The returned exiles use it to answer an official challenge by appealing to history: We are the servants of the God of heaven and earth, and build the house that was builded these many years ago, which a great king of Israel builded and set up (Ezra 5:11).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines AGO as past; gone; used after a noun of time, as, a year ago, long ago.
webster_full: AGO, adv. — Past; gone; as, ten years ago.
It is always used after a noun expressing a portion of time.
AGONE, the older form, now obsolete except in poetry.
Middle English agon, past participle of agon, to go away or pass.
Anglo-Saxon agan, to pass away.
scriptures: Matthew 11:21
Woe unto thee, Chorazin! woe unto thee, Bethsaida! for if the mighty works, which were done in you, had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago in sackcloth and ashes.
2 Corinthians 12:2
I knew a man in Christ above fourteen years ago, (whether in the body, I cannot tell; or whether out of the body, I cannot tell: God knoweth;) such an one caught up to the third heaven.
Ezra 5:11

And thus they returned us answer, saying, We are the servants of the God of heaven and earth, and build the house that was builded these many years ago, which a great king of Israel builded and set up.
Matthew 11:22
But I say unto you, It shall be more tolerable for Tyre and Sidon at the day of judgment, than for you.
corruption_summary: Matthew 11:21-22 teaches degrees of judgment proportioned to light received, which neither the flattening of all sin into one undifferentiated mass nor the denial of judgment altogether can accommodate.
corruption_paragraphs: Our Lord says it shall be more tolerable for Tyre and Sidon in the day of judgment than for Chorazin and Bethsaida, and He says the same of Sodom against Capernaum. Judgment is therefore proportioned to light received: greater privilege carries greater accountability, and the towns that watched His miracles and did not repent stand in a worse case than the pagan cities the prophets condemned. This cuts two ways. Against the denial of judgment, it insists on a day and a reckoning with real gradations. And against the loose talk that treats all sin as simply equal, it maintains that while all sin deserves wrath, not all sin incurs the same degree of it — a distinction the 1689 Confession makes explicitly. The practical weight falls on those with the most exposure to the word, which in the modern West means almost everyone who has heard and shrugged.

2 Corinthians 12:2 is a rebuke to a whole genre. Paul waited fourteen years before mentioning being caught up to the third heaven, referred to himself in the third person when he did, declined to say whether he was in the body, and refused to report what he heard because it was unlawful to utter. He mentions it at all only because the Corinthians had forced him into a comparison with the false apostles, and he immediately turns to the thorn in the flesh and glories in his infirmities instead. Set against the modern market in heaven-visitation narratives — detailed, promoted, and sold — the contrast is not a matter of taste. The apostle’s reticence is theological: he would not have men think of him above what they saw him to be, and the sufficiency of Scripture leaves nothing for such reports to add.
roots_summary: Greek palai (G3819), long ago, of old; pro etous, before a year, in the phrase fourteen years ago; Aramaic qadmath, formerly, aforetime.
roots_lines: Greek palai (G3819) — long ago, of old; they would have repented long ago (Matthew 11:21).
Greek pro eton dekatessaron — fourteen years before; Paul’s dating of the vision (2 Corinthians 12:2).
Greek anektoteros (G414) — more tolerable, more endurable; the comparison of judgments (Matthew 11:22).
Greek arrhetos (G731) — unspeakable, not to be uttered; what Paul heard and would not report (2 Corinthians 12:4).
Aramaic shenin saggian — many years; the exiles’ appeal to the temple’s antiquity (Ezra 5:11).
usage: They would have repented long ago in sackcloth and ashes (Matthew 11:21) — pagan cities on evidence the Galilean towns shrugged at.
It shall be more tolerable for Tyre and Sidon at the day of judgment, than for you (Matthew 11:22) — judgment proportioned to light.
I knew a man in Christ above fourteen years ago (2 Corinthians 12:2) — fourteen years of silence about the extraordinary.

etymology: From Latin sors, a lot, and so a share, a class, a kind, through French sorte. Webster 1828: a kind, species or class; manner, form of being or acting. Paul uses it of men who creep into houses, and Acts of the men who started a riot.
biblical_def: The word classifies, and Scripture uses it to classify men. Paul warns Timothy of a specific type and describes their method: of this sort are they which creep into houses, and lead captive silly women laden with sins, led away with divers lusts (2 Timothy 3:6) — the approach is private rather than public, the target is chosen for vulnerability, and the mechanism is captivity rather than persuasion. Luke names the recruits of the Thessalonian mob with equal plainness: the Jews which believed not, moved with envy, took unto them certain lewd fellows of the baser sort, and gathered a company, and set all the city on an uproar (Acts 17:5) — envy at the top and hired roughness at the bottom, which is how such uproars are generally assembled. Paul also uses the phrase of his own manner of writing: I have written the more boldly unto you in some sort, as putting you in mind, because of the grace that is given to me of God (Romans 15:15) — boldness exercised, and immediately accounted for by grace rather than by office.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines SORT as a kind or species; any number or collection of individual persons or things characterized by the same or like qualities; also manner, form of being or acting.
webster_full: SORT, n. — A kind or species; any number or collection of individual persons or things characterized by the same or like qualities.
Manner; form of being or acting; as, in some sort.
Class or order; as men of the baser sort.
SORT, v.t. — To separate and place in distinct classes or divisions.
Latin sors, a lot, hence a share or class — the root of sortition and assort.
scriptures: 2 Timothy 3:6
For of this sort are they which creep into houses, and lead captive silly women laden with sins, led away with divers lusts,
Acts 17:5

But the Jews which believed not, moved with envy, took unto them certain lewd fellows of the baser sort, and gathered a company, and set all the city on an uproar, and assaulted the house of Jason, and sought to bring them out to the people.
Romans 15:15
Nevertheless, brethren, I have written the more boldly unto you in some sort, as putting you in mind, because of the grace that is given to me of God,
2 Timothy 3:7
Ever learning, and never able to come to the knowledge of the truth.
corruption_summary: 2 Timothy 3:6-7 describes a predator’s method precisely — private access, chosen vulnerability, endless learning without arrival — and the church has repeatedly failed to recognise it because it expects the danger to be public.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul’s description is operational rather than merely moral. These men creep into houses: the access is private, obtained gradually, and outside the assembly where elders could see it. They target the vulnerable — the Greek is a diminutive, and the point is not that women are foolish but that these particular ones were burdened with sin and led by their appetites, which is the condition the predator looks for. And the result is captivity, with the victims ever learning, and never able to come to the knowledge of the truth: a permanent dependence on the teacher rather than an arrival at truth that would set them free of him. The church’s repeated failure to see this pattern has come from expecting false teaching to arrive as public heresy. It arrives as private attention, and the elders’ duty of oversight extends to what happens in houses.

Acts 17:5 is worth naming for its anatomy of a mob. The instigators are described as moved with envy — a motive they would not have avowed — and the muscle is recruited from certain lewd fellows of the baser sort, men with no stake in the theological question at all. The charge finally laid was political: these that have turned the world upside down do contrary to the decrees of Caesar, saying that there is another king, one Jesus (Acts 17:6-7). Envy at the top, hired disorder at the bottom, and a civil accusation in the middle, because the real objection could not be stated. It is a pattern worth recognising when the church is opposed, and it should make believers careful to give no occasion for the civil charge, since the accusation in Thessalonica was, in the deepest sense, true.
roots_summary: Greek toutos in the phrase of this sort; agoraios (G60), of the marketplace, a loafer; meros (G3313), a part, in the phrase in some sort; Latin sors, a lot.
roots_lines: Greek agoraios (G60) — belonging to the marketplace, a loiterer; lewd fellows of the baser sort (Acts 17:5).
Greek meros (G3313) — a part or measure; in some sort, that is, in some measure (Romans 15:15).
Greek enduno (G1744) — to slip in, to creep in; the method of 2 Timothy 3:6.
Greek aichmaloteuo (G162) — to lead captive as a prisoner of war; the result of that method.
Greek epignosis (G1922) — full knowledge; what the captives never reach (2 Timothy 3:7).
usage: Of this sort are they which creep into houses (2 Timothy 3:6) — private access, chosen vulnerability, captivity as the aim.
Ever learning, and never able to come to the knowledge of the truth (2 Timothy 3:7) — dependence maintained by never arriving.
Certain lewd fellows of the baser sort (Acts 17:5) — envy at the top and hired roughness at the bottom.
